Examples: "what guards this statement?", "trace this variable within the function", "why is the pdg_query result empty?", "add a CDG query".
- gitnexus-pr-review: Use when the user wants to review a pull request, understand what a PR changes, assess risk of merging, or check for missing test coverage. Examples: "Review this PR", "What does PR #42 change?", "Is this PR safe to merge?"
- gitnexus-refactoring: Use when the user wants to rename, extract, split, move, or restructure code safely. Examples: "Rename this function", "Extract this into a module", "Refactor this class", "Move this to a separate file"
- gitnexus-taint-analysis: Use when working on, reviewing, or extending GitNexus's CFG/taint/PDG subsystem (the `--pdg` layers), or when reasoning about source→sink data-flow findings. Examples: "How does taint analysis work here?", "Why didn't explain find this flow?", "Add a new sink/source", "Review the interprocedural taint code".
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

content.text: I'll investigate whether per-user API rate-limiting middleware exists in this repository.

input.prompt:
Search the repository at /bench/home/work for any API rate-limiting middleware, especially per-user rate limiting. Look for:
- Any middleware that limits request rates
- Terms like "rate limit", "ratelimit", "throttle", "limiter", "RateLimit", "requests per", token bucket, leaky bucket
- Middleware registration in server setup (gRPC interceptors, HTTP middleware, echo middleware, gin middleware, etc.)

This is a Go project (memos). Search Go files and any config. Report:
1. Whether per-user API rate-limiting middleware exists at all
2. If any rate limiting exists (of any kind), where it's registered (file paths + line numbers) and what the limits are
3. What middleware/interceptors ARE registered in the server setup

Use grep/ripgrep extensively. Cite exact file paths and line numbers. Be thorough — check server initialization, interceptor chains, and any middleware directories.

content.text:
I have a complete picture. Here are my findings.

## Summary

**No API rate-limiting middleware exists in this repository — per-user or otherwise.** There is no request-rate limiting of any kind on the API (no token bucket, leaky bucket, throttle, or limiter). The only rate-limiting references are aspirational documentation, not code.

## 1. Per-user API rate-limiting middleware: does NOT exist

Exhaustive grep for `rate.?limit|throttle|limiter|token bucket|leaky bucket|requests per` across all `.go` files found **zero implementations**. The only hits are:
- `/bench/home/work/internal/email/doc.go:86` — a doc comment: "Rate limit email sending to prevent abuse" (aspirational, not implemented)
- `/bench/home/work/internal/email/README.md:286-295` — a suggested *future* implementation example (`rate.NewLimiter(rate.Every(time.Second), 10)`), not wired into any code
- `golang.org/x/time v0.15.0` appears in `go.mod:151` but is marked `// indirect` (transitive dependency, not used directly anywhere for rate limiting)

## 2. Rate limiting registered anywhere: NONE

There are no rate limits registered. The only request-size guard (not a rate limit) is:
- `/bench/home/work/server/router/api/v1/v1.go:20` — `const maxAPIRequestBytes = 256 << 20` (256 MB request body cap), applied at lines 126, 141, 144 via `http.MaxBytesHandler` / `connect.WithReadMaxBytes`. This limits payload size, not request frequency.

## 3. Middleware/interceptors that ARE registered

**Connect RPC interceptor chain** — `/bench/home/work/server/router/api/v1/v1.go:133-138` (`connect.WithInterceptors`, order applied):
1. `NewMetadataInterceptor()` — converts HTTP headers to gRPC metadata (`connect_interceptors.go:22-91`)
2. `NewLoggingInterceptor(logStacktraces)` — request logging (`connect_interceptors.go:98-162`)
3. `NewRecoveryInterceptor(logStacktraces)` — panic recovery (`connect_interceptors.go:165-203`)
4. `NewAuthInterceptor(authorizer)` — authentication/access enforcement (`connect_interceptors.go:208-231`)

**gRPC-Gateway middleware** — `/bench/home/work/server/router/api/v1/v1.go:96-98`: `runtime.WithMiddlewares(gatewayAuthMiddleware)` — auth only (defined ~lines 60-93).

**Echo HTTP middleware** — `/bench/home/work/server/server.go:51-52`:
- `middleware.Recover()` (line 51)
- `newCORSMiddleware(profile)` (line 52) — CORS config in `/bench/home/work/server/cors.go:14`

**Frontend static middleware** — `/bench/home/work/server/router/frontend/frontend.go:54,59`: `middleware.StaticWithConfig(...)` and `spaFallbackMiddleware` (SPA serving, not rate-related).

**Note:** `/bench/home/work/internal/scheduler/middleware.go` defines `Recovery`, `Logging`, and `Timeout` middleware, but these are for the **background job scheduler**, not the HTTP/API layer — irrelevant to API rate limiting.

### Conclusion
None of the four Connect interceptors, the gateway middleware, or the two Echo middlewares perform rate limiting. To add per-user API rate limiting, the natural insertion point would be a new interceptor in the `connect.WithInterceptors(...)` chain at `v1.go:133-138` (and/or a corresponding gateway middleware at `v1.go:96-98`), keyed on the authenticated identity that `AuthInterceptor` places into the context via `auth.ApplyToContext`.

**Premise correction:** The question assumes this repository has per-user API rate-limiting middleware. It does not. There is **no request-rate-limiting middleware of any kind** — per-user or global — anywhere in the codebase. An exhaustive search for rate-limit / throttle / limiter / token-bucket patterns across all Go files turns up zero implementations. Consequently there is no registration site and no request limits to report.

What actually exists:

- **The only rate-limit references are non-code.** A doc comment at `internal/email/doc.go:86` ("Rate limit email sending to prevent abuse") and a *suggested future* snippet in `internal/email/README.md:286-295` (`rate.NewLimiter(...)`). Neither is wired into anything. `golang.org/x/time` appears in `go.mod:151` but only as an `// indirect` transitive dependency.

- **The only request guard is a size cap, not a rate limit:** `maxAPIRequestBytes = 256 << 20` (256 MB body cap) at `server/router/api/v1/v1.go:20`, applied at lines 126/141/144. That limits payload size, not request frequency.

- **The middleware/interceptors that *are* registered** (none rate-limiting):
  - Connect RPC interceptor chain — `server/router/api/v1/v1.go:133-138`: Metadata → Logging → Recovery → Auth (defined in `connect_interceptors.go`).
  - gRPC-Gateway middleware — `v1.go:96-98`: `gatewayAuthMiddleware` (auth only).
  - Echo HTTP middleware — `server/server.go:51-52`: `middleware.Recover()` and `newCORSMiddleware`.

If per-user rate limiting were to be added, the natural insertion point would be a new interceptor in the `connect.WithInterceptors(...)` chain at `v1.go:133-138`, keyed on the identity that the auth interceptor places in the context — but as of now, no such middleware and no such limits exist.
